doc.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

chapter: New York work and early influences
title: Lou McGarity and trombone influences
summary: Hearing McGarity's solo on Yours led him to trombone; he learned Goodman sextet choruses and listened to other swing trombonists.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Well you know we kind of skipped over some early influences. You mentioned that your father was a musician and had a family orientation there with the music. The trombone players — I think I read that Cutty Cutshall and Lou McGarity were people that you aspired to.

Lou was responsible for me playing trombone. I just heard his recording of “Yours” with the Benny Goodman Orchestra, I think it was 1941 or ‘42. He played an eight bar solo there, and I heard it and I said that’s what I want to play.
Eight bars and you knew what you wanted to do. That’s saying something.

It was such a driving force but so musical. And from that point on I got all the Goodman sextet records with Lou and learned all his choruses note for note, which is a great way to start I think. Eventually we all hope that we can be ourselves. And we have something that identifies us. But to begin with, you’ve got to hear something you like and you’ve got to hear a style that you like. Plus there were so many great players in those days, you know there was Jack Teagarden and Cutty Cutshall and Bill Harris and Jack Jenny and Trummy Young. I mean I had all these great players to listen to. It was a wonderful time to grow up.
